scenes.narration: Here is what raise does. The error starts inside the function, at the line that raised it. The function stops there. The error travels up to the caller, and looks for a matching except. If it finds one, that block runs. If not, it keeps travelling, and finally stops the program with a traceback. You decide who handles the error.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: the except blocks are in the wrong order
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We have a value error block, but the output says general. Python tries the except blocks in order, and uses the first match. Exception matches every error, so it wins, and the value error block never runs. Put the most specific block first, and the general one last.

props.why: Python uses the first except that matches, and Exception matches everything, so a later more specific block never runs.

challenge: Write check_score(score) that raises ValueError if score is above 100, and test it with 120.
challengeAnswer: Use def check_score(score): if score > 100: raise ValueError("score too high"), then wrap check_score(120) in try and except ValueError.

shorts.title: Raise
shorts.script: You can raise an error yourself. Raise, an exception type, and a message. Raise value error, age cannot be negative. The function stops at that line, and the error travels up to the nearest except. Think of a referee blowing a whistle when a rule is broken. Use raise when your function receives a value it cannot accept. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Blow the whistle.

shorts.title: Except as e
shorts.hook: "To read the error message, add as e to the except line."
shorts.script: To read the error message, add as e to the except line. Except value error as e. Now e holds the error object. Printing e shows the message you passed to raise. It is a good way to tell the user what went wrong, in your own words. It also helps when you log errors, to find bugs later. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Read the message.

shorts.title: Your own exception
shorts.hook: "You can make your own type of exception."
shorts.script: You can make your own type of exception. Write class, a name, then Exception in brackets, and a colon, and the word pass. That is the whole thing. Now you can raise it, and catch it by name. It makes your code read clearly, because bill error says exactly what went wrong, better than a plain value error. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: A custom error type.

shorts.title: Order of except blocks
shorts.script: Here is a quiet bug. You write an except for exception first, and an except for value error after it. Python uses the first match. Exception matches everything, so it wins, and the second block never runs. No error, only the wrong message. Put the most specific block first, and the general one last. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Order matters.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.hook: "Why was the referee so good at coding?"
shorts.script: Why was the referee so good at coding? It knew when to raise a flag. Your challenge. Write a function called check score, that raises a value error if the score is above one hundred. Then call it with one twenty inside a try block, and print the error message in the except block. Share your code in the comments below. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 55.
